text: vector, direct access, and sparse storage with map.

A linear list keeps items in a row, each with one item before it and one after. The four structures of this chapter store such a row differently, and each makes different operations cheap. Choose by the operations the problem needs most.

105 lockers with up to 105 slots each would need 1010 boxes, but only q of them are ever used. A map stores only the used (key, value) pairs, each lookup costs O(log q) (P3613).
map[key] creates the key with value 0 if it is missing; that is exactly "empty slot" here. Use map.count(key) when you must not create it.
Last in, first out: postfix expressions, brackets, stack sequences.
push / pop at the top
A stack is last in, first out (LIFO): you only touch the top, like a pile of plates. push puts on top, pop removes the top, top reads it; all O(1).
Use a stack when the most recent unfinished thing must be dealt with first: matching brackets, evaluating expressions, undoing steps, and turning recursion into a loop.

In postfix (后缀) notation the operator comes after its two operands, so no brackets are needed. Push numbers; on an operator, pop two, combine, push the result. The last value on the stack is the answer (P1449).
The first pop is the right operand. For - and / the order matters: 5 2 − means 5 − 2.

Brackets: each closer must match the most recent unmatched opener, which is the stack top; at the end nothing may be left (P1241 adds rules for repairing). Stack sequences: simulate with a real stack, popping whenever the top is the next value to pop; if anything is left, the order was impossible (P4387).
First in, first out: Josephus circle and a fixed-size memory.
front pops first, new items join at the back
A queue is first in, first out (FIFO), like a line at a counter. push joins at the back, pop leaves from the front, front reads the first; all O(1).
BFS (第14章) is a queue. deque allows push and pop at both ends, useful for sliding windows such as "ships in the last 24 hours" (P2058).

A circle of people counting off becomes a queue: moving the front to the back is "pass to the next person" (P1996). A memory that forgets the oldest item is a queue plus a marking array that answers "is it stored?" in O(1) (P1540).
Links in L[] and R[] arrays: O(1) insert and delete.
head 2 4 1 R[x] = right neighbour, L[x] = left neighbour

A linked list stores, for every item, who comes next (and, doubly linked, who comes before). Inserting or deleting only rewires a few links: O(1), with no shifting. The price: reaching the i-th item means walking from the head, O(n).
In contests, keep the links in two arrays, L[x] and R[x] , indexed by the item itself; node 0 is a fixed head that is never deleted, so the first item needs no special case.

"Insert left of k" is "insert right of k's left neighbour", so one insert function is enough. Delete by linking the two neighbours to each other. Walking R[] from the head prints the final order (P1160).
Step Links changed insert x right of k R[x], L[x], L[R[k]], R[k] delete x R[L[x]], L[R[x]] walk x = R[x] until back at head 0
Rewire in the right order: read R[k] into x's links before overwriting R[k] .
Drawing the boxes and arrows on paper first prevents most linked-list bugs.
For "closest earlier value" questions such as daily turnover (P2234), a sorted set with lower_bound gives each answer in O(log n) (集合 , 第17章).
The Luogu problems for this chapter, a ladder through them, and experiments to try yourself.
Key points to memorise
1. Pick the structure by its cheap operations: index → array; ends → stack/queue; middle → linked list.
2. vector: push_back O(1), v[i] O(1), insert/erase in the middle O(n).
3. Sparse huge index space → map; map[key] creates a 0 if missing.
4. stack: push, pop, top; LIFO; brackets, postfix, undo.
5. Postfix: push numbers; on an operator pop b then a, push a op b.
6. Brackets: closer must match the top; stack must end empty.
7. queue: push, pop, front; FIFO; BFS, circles, caches.
8. Josephus: move the front to the back m − 1 times, then remove.
9. Linked list in arrays: L[x], R[x], head node 0; insert/delete O(1).
10. Insert-left of k = insert-right of L[k]; delete = link the two neighbours.
